findings.claim: All 84 practice questions are set in forms this section does not use: 24 x '4 marks - Describe Two Features', 15 x '8 marks - Explain Effects', 17 x '8 marks - Explain Significance', 1 x '4 marks - Two Ways Similar or Different', 12 x '16 marks - Period Argument' and 3 x '16 marks - Source-Based Essay'. Only the four narrative accounts (Lessons 5, 7, 13 and 14) are in a form this section sets, and not one interpretation question appears anywhere in the unit.
findings.truth: The British depth study on this paper sets four questions worth 40 marks: an 8-mark interpretation question ('How convincing is Interpretation A about...?'), an 8-mark 'Explain what was important about...', an 8-mark 'Write an account of...', and a 16-mark essay on the specified historic environment site. 'Describe two features' is an Edexcel form; 'Explain the significance of' and 'Explain two ways in which... were similar/different' belong to the thematic study in the other half of this paper; no sources are supplied in this section, so a source-based essay cannot be set here.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Section B table (four questions: interpretation 8, explain 8, account 8, site essay 16) and 2.2 (Paper 2, 2 hours, 84 marks, Section B four compulsory questions, 40 marks)

findings.claim: 'Ten were hanged, drawn and quartered at Charing Cross.'
findings.truth: Ten regicides were executed in October 1660, but Daniel Axtell and Francis Hacker died at Tyburn, not Charing Cross.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Regicides of Charles I' (executions of October 1660)

findings.claim: Eight exam tips coach forms this section does not set - 'Explain Effects', 'Describe Two Features', 'Explain Significance' - and several add unevidenced claims about marking ('Markers want two features clearly separated', 'examiners want consequences', 'Markers reward both timescales explicitly', 'markers reward consequences, not background'). Lesson 1 also tells students to use precise vocabulary 'to access the SPaG marks across the paper'.
findings.truth: Rewritten for the forms this section sets, with the marker claims removed. This section carries no spelling, punctuation and grammar marks (see F37).
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Section B table and the description of the four Section B questions

findings.claim: Seven flashcard answers are enumerations the validator rejects, for example 'Cromwell, Ireton and Bradshaw.', 'The monarchy, the House of Lords and the Church of England.', 'Corporation Act 1661, Act of Uniformity 1662, Conventicle Act 1664 and Five Mile Act 1665.', '1679, 1680 and 1681.' and 'Rights to fortify, mint money, raise troops, hold courts and make peace with non-Christian princes.'
findings.truth: Rewritten one idea per card, with the question reshaped to match.
findings.evidence: house flashcard rules (an answer must not be a list of items)

findings.claim: 'Quakers, founded by George Fox... were jailed in their thousands - including the writer John Bunyan, imprisoned in Bedford gaol from 1660 to 1672 where he wrote The Pilgrim's Progress.'
findings.truth: Bunyan was not a Quaker. He belonged to the Bedford Meeting and argued in print against the Quakers. He began The Pilgrim's Progress in gaol but published it in 1678.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'John Bunyan'

findings.claim: 'The Crown received an initial GBP 225,000 from Louis.'
findings.truth: The Dover money was promised, not received on signature: two million crowns for the Catholic declaration and a yearly subsidy while the Dutch war lasted. The lesson's figure is the annual war subsidy, not a lump sum.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Secret Treaty of Dover' (two million crowns for the declaration; an annual secret pension)

findings.claim: 'The discovery of the Rye House Plot in 1683 allowed Charles to purge Whig sympathisers from corporations' and 'Beginning with London in 1683, the government used quo warranto writs'.
findings.truth: The quo warranto campaign began before the plot. The writ against the City of London was issued in 1681 and judgment came in June 1683; the plot let Charles press an existing campaign harder.
findings.evidence: spec Part one (rule without parliament from 1681) plus the standard chronology of the London quo warranto case

findings.claim: 'James II, when he succeeded in February 1685, inherited a Parliament of Tory loyalists' and 'James II inherited a Parliament of constituencies stacked with Tories.'
findings.truth: No Parliament existed in February 1685 - the lesson itself says Charles summoned none after March 1681. James called elections in spring 1685 and those returned a Tory Parliament.
findings.evidence: internal (Lessons 3 and 8 both date the personal rule from March 1681 to February 1685)

findings.claim: Catherine of Braganza's dowry is given twice as 'GBP 360,000 in cash'.
findings.truth: The cash dowry was two million Portuguese crowns, valued at about GBP 300,000.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Charles II of England' ('two million Portuguese crowns (equivalent to GBP 300,000 then)') and 'Catherine of Braganza'

findings.claim: 'fathered at least fourteen illegitimate children'
findings.truth: Charles II acknowledged at least twelve illegitimate children.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Charles II of England'

findings.claim: 'Sir Roger L'Estrange ran the Surveyor of the Press from 1663'
findings.truth: L'Estrange held the office of Surveyor of the Press; as written the sentence states nothing.
findings.evidence: internal (the sentence is not a statement of fact)

findings.claim: 'By August deaths were running at over 7,000 a week, the court had fled to Oxford', repeated in the exam tip as 'the peak in August-September with the court's flight to Oxford'.
findings.truth: Weekly deaths passed 7,000 in September, not August. The court left for Salisbury in July and only moved to Oxford in September - as the lesson itself says four paragraphs later.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Great Plague of London' (over 7,000 per week in September; court to Salisbury in July, Oxford in September)

findings.claim: 'Cold weather killed off the fleas; surviving rats had built immunity' (L5) and 'the Plague did not return on the 1665 scale, partly because brick and stone gave rats fewer hiding places' (L6).
findings.truth: Both are contested hypotheses stated as fact, and Lesson 5 itself says the reasons plague did not return are still debated. The Fire also destroyed only the walled City, while the worst plague parishes lay outside it.
findings.evidence: internal (Lesson 5: 'why is still debated')

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward analytical narrative; lists of events with no causal explanation cap in the middle band' and 'lists of events without causal links cap in the middle band'.
findings.truth: No published source supports either claim about how answers are banded.
findings.evidence: house rule on unevidenced examiner claims

findings.claim: 'four of the City's gates'
findings.truth: Three western gates burned: Ludgate, Newgate and Aldersgate.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Great Fire of London'

findings.claim: 'The Monument to the Fire, completed in 1677, originally carried a Latin inscription blaming the treachery and malice of the Popish faction', repeated in the match set as 'originally inscribed against the Popish faction'.
findings.truth: The anti-Catholic inscription was cut in 1681, years after the Monument was finished, at the height of the Exclusion Crisis.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Great Fire of London' (inscription added 1681, removed 1830)

findings.claim: 'The hearth tax was redirected to fund firefighting equipment'
findings.truth: No published source supports this. The rebuilding fund was the coal duty imposed by the Rebuilding Acts, which the same sentence goes on to describe.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Great Fire of London' (Rebuilding Acts and the coal tax)

findings.claim: Two exam tips and three practice questions coach a '16 marks - Source-Based Essay' on this section, telling students to 'use the source(s) and your own knowledge together' and that 'Markers reward integrated argument with embedded source detail'.
findings.truth: This section supplies no sources and sets no source question. Its 16-mark question is the essay on the specified historic environment site; source questions belong to the thematic study in the other half of the paper and to the other paper.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.2, Section B table and question descriptions (the first Section B question is an interpretation tested on AO4; the final one is the site essay)

findings.claim: 'popery' is defined, in the article dfn and in the glossary, as 'Hostility towards the Roman Catholic Church and its followers'.
findings.truth: Popery is a hostile Protestant word for Roman Catholicism itself. The definition inverts the term, so the sentence a student hovers reads 'the fear of hostility towards the Catholic Church ran deep'.
findings.evidence: standard usage; internal (the sentence is 'The fear of popery ran deep')

findings.claim: 'the Second Test Act of 1678, barring Catholics from sitting in either House of Parliament - a clause aimed at James himself, who had to leave the Lords' and 'Around 35 Catholics were executed between 1678 and 1681'.
findings.truth: The 1678 Act carried a proviso exempting James, Duke of York, so he kept his seat in the Lords. Executions are counted at at least 22; the higher figures count deaths in prison as well.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Test Act' ('managed to greatly weaken it by including an exemption for the future James II') and 'Popish Plot' ('the executions of at least 22 men')

findings.claim: 'Whigs argued that Parliament had the right to determine the succession...; the strongest, in their view, were the constitutional rights settled in 1660.'
findings.truth: The second clause is unfinished and asserts constitutional rights 'settled in 1660' that the Restoration settlement did not settle - Lesson 1 says the opposite.
findings.evidence: internal (Lesson 1: the settlement postponed rather than solved the constitutional questions)

findings.claim: 'Top-band answers can use these sources to show that the Crisis was a contest of ideas' (L8 article text), 'a connection examiners reward' (L14 article text) and 'the examiner sees a student in control of the chronology' (L14 exam tip).
findings.truth: Unevidenced claims about examiner behaviour, two of them inside the article itself. The L8 case is also wrong about the paper: Marvell, Filmer and Locke are not exam sources.
findings.evidence: house rule on unevidenced examiner claims; spec 4.4.2

findings.claim: The match set labels the third position 'Court party (Halifax)' against the answer 'Trim between the two sides to keep the constitution balanced'.
findings.truth: Halifax was a trimmer who opposed exclusion; the Court party label belongs to Danby's grouping, which Lesson 3 defines.
findings.evidence: internal (Lesson 3 glossary defines the Court party as Danby's Anglican royalist grouping)

findings.claim: In a passage about the 1670s: 'Lloyd's in Lombard Street became the centre of marine insurance, Jonathan's the heart of stock-jobbing in the City', repeated in a practice mark scheme and a flashcard.
findings.truth: Lloyd's opened in Tower Street in 1686, after Charles II's death, and only moved to Lombard Street in 1691. Jonathan's opened about 1680 and drew the stock-jobbers in the 1690s.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Lloyd's Coffee House' and 'Jonathan's Coffee-House'

findings.claim: Pope is quoted as 'the stage how loosely does Astrea tread'.
findings.truth: Pope wrote 'The stage how loosely does Astraea tread'.
findings.evidence: Pope, 'The First Epistle of the Second Book of Horace' (1737)

findings.claim: 'some at Wadham College Oxford under John Wilkins during the Civil War' and 'John Wilkins... ran the original wartime experimental club'.
findings.truth: Wilkins became Warden of Wadham in 1648 and the Oxford experimental club met through the 1650s, after the fighting had ended. It was an Interregnum body, not a wartime one.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Royal Society' and 'John Wilkins'

findings.claim: 'He was elected President in December 1684, a year before the death of Charles II'.
findings.truth: Charles II died on 6 February 1685, two months after Pepys was elected.
findings.evidence: internal (Lesson 12 dates the death to 6 February 1685)

findings.claim: 'Newton, when President from 1703, removed every reference to Hooke from the Society's rooms and possibly arranged for Hooke's portrait to be lost.'
findings.truth: No authenticated portrait of Hooke has ever been identified, and Hooke's biographer Allan Chapman rejects the destruction story as a myth.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Robert Hooke' ('Chapman rejects as a myth claims Newton or his acolytes deliberately destroyed Hooke's portrait')

findings.claim: 'used Sir Peter Lely (court painter from 1661) to produce the famous Windsor Beauties portrait series'.
findings.truth: The Windsor Beauties were commissioned by Anne Hyde, Duchess of York, not by Charles II.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Windsor Beauties'

findings.claim: 'Who was Robert Boyle's most famous scientific contribution?' answered 'Boyle's Law of gases, published in 1662.'
findings.truth: The question should ask 'What was...'.
findings.evidence: internal

findings.claim: 'the Second Treaty of Westminster, two years before France finished its own war', repeated in a practice mark scheme.
findings.truth: England left in February 1674; France and the Dutch Republic made peace at Nijmegen in 1678, four years later.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Franco-Dutch War'

findings.claim: 'Charles II danced between the two: he allied with France against the Dutch under the Treaty of Dover, but was forced by Parliament to sign the Triple Alliance with the Dutch and Sweden against France in 1668.'
findings.truth: The sequence is inverted. The Triple Alliance was signed in January 1668, two years before the Treaty of Dover, and it was negotiated by Sir William Temple for the Crown, not forced on Charles by Parliament.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Triple Alliance (1668)' (signed 23 January 1668; Temple the driving force)

findings.claim: 'its main use to England was as the source of the privateering commissions that legitimised raids on its Caribbean colonies' - said of Spain.
findings.truth: Spain was the target of the raids. The commissions were issued by the governors of Jamaica, as Lesson 12 says.
findings.evidence: internal (Lesson 12: Morgan 'attacked Spanish settlements under commissions from the governor of Jamaica')

findings.claim: 'When was the first Restoration Navigation Act passed?' answered '1660, by the Cavalier Parliament.'
findings.truth: The Act passed on 13 September 1660, in the Convention Parliament. The Cavalier Parliament, elected in 1661, only confirmed it in July 1661.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Navigation Acts'

findings.claim: 'a large mole (a stone breakwater) which Pepys oversaw on a 1683 inspection visit... In 1684 Charles ordered the garrison evacuated and the mole blown up'.
findings.truth: Pepys sailed with Lord Dartmouth in 1683 to wind Tangier up, not to oversee the mole's construction. The order to abandon was given in 1683 and the evacuation was completed in early 1684.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'English Tangier' and 'Samuel Pepys' (the 1683 Dartmouth expedition)

findings.claim: 'Between 1672 and 1685 the Company shipped roughly 90,000 enslaved Africans across the Atlantic', repeated four times across the lesson.
findings.truth: The Royal African Company's ships carried 186,748 people between 1672 and 1731, and about 5,000 a year in the 1680s. The 90,000 figure covers a much longer span than Charles II's reign.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Royal African Company' ('Between 1672 and 1731... 186,748 enslaved people'; 'In the 1680s, the company was transporting about 5,000 enslaved people a year')

findings.claim: Twelve 16-mark mark schemes end '[16 marks + 4 SPaG]', and the sibling Elizabethan unit's applied edits make the same claim on its two site essays.
findings.truth: Two readings. (a) Follow the specification, which is the authority on exam structure: its Section B table gives the site essay a total of 16 with no SPaG figure, and the sentence 'Marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar will also be available' appears in the Section A and Paper 1 Section B question descriptions but NOT in the Section B site-essay description. The arithmetic only works this way - Section A 8+8+8+16 plus 4 SPaG = 44, Section B 8+8+8+16 = 40, paper total 84. (b) Follow the sibling unit and keep the SPaG claim. I have taken (a) and written every tariff line as plain '[16 marks - ...]'. If Tom prefers (b), the Elizabethan unit already matches it and this unit needs twelve tariff lines changed back. Either way the two units must agree.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 (Paper 2: 84 marks including 4 for SPaG; Section A 40, Section B 40, plus 4 SPaG) and 4.4.2 (Section A table total 20 for its essay versus Section B table total 16 for the site essay)
findings.ruling: Accepted: Paper 2 SPaG belongs to the Section A thematic essay; site essays are 16 marks plain. The Elizabethan, Norman and Edward I units are being swept to match.

findings.claim: 'estimates suggest he had perhaps 200 MPs receiving Crown money in some form' - said of Danby.
findings.truth: No figure could be verified from the sources available here. Left as written.
findings.evidence: not verified

findings.claim: 'Around half of London's clergy fled'.
findings.truth: No figure could be verified from the sources available here. Left as written.
findings.evidence: not verified

findings.claim: Both lessons tell students the Medway is 'your specified site for 2027' and St Paul's 'your specified site for the 2028 exam'.
findings.truth: The board publishes the specified site three years in advance and the specification does not name it. Neither claim can be checked from the sources available here; both should be confirmed against the board's published site list before each series.
findings.evidence: spec, Part four ('For all series the specified site will be published three years in advance')

findings.claim: 'more than five people outside one household' - the Conventicle Act threshold, repeated in the glossary, a key fact, a match set, a flashcard and two mark schemes.
findings.truth: The statute reads 'five persons or more assembled together (other than those of the same household)', so a meeting of exactly five outsiders was already illegal. The lesson's wording matches the standard textbook simplification and the ripple would touch seven fields, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Conventicle Act 1664'

findings.claim: 'branded with the Duke of York's initials DY on the chest'.
findings.truth: Sources give both 'DY' and 'DoY'. Left as written.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Royal African Company' ('branded with the letters DoY')

findings.claim: 'By 1685 enslaved Africans outnumbered white settlers on Jamaica by roughly four to one.'
findings.truth: The ratio could not be verified for 1685 from the sources available here; it is closer to four to one by the 1690s. Left as written.
findings.evidence: not verified

summary: Every one of the 84 practice questions was set in a form this section does not use, and the unit carried no interpretation question at all. All 84 are converted to the four forms the British depth study sets, with rebuilt mark schemes; the two historic-environment lessons now carry two site essays each. Beyond that: the glossary inverts 'popery'; the 1678 Test Act is said to have forced James from the Lords when a proviso exempted him; the Triple Alliance is placed after the Treaty of Dover and blamed on Parliament; figures are corrected (dowry, illegitimate children, city gates, Popish Plot executions, Royal African Company volumes); chronology is corrected (plague peak, Tangier evacuation, Nijmegen, the quo warranto campaign, James II's first Parliament); three fabrications are removed (hearth tax redirected to firefighting, Newton destroying Hooke's portrait, Charles II commissioning the Windsor Beauties); eleven unevidenced examiner claims are cut. One ADJUDICATE: whether this section's 16-mark site essay carries 4 SPaG marks - the specification says it does not, the sibling Elizabethan unit says it does.
